## Abstract

**Background.** Extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma (EMC) usually carries an *EWSR1*::*NR4A3* gene fusion. Its junction joins sequences from two parent proteins and may provide a target for a cancer vaccine. Human studies in other fusion-driven sarcomas show that junction-peptide vaccines can be administered and can produce T-cell responses [17,18,19,20]. They do not establish benefit, and none concerns EMC. A positive phase 3 melanoma result has been announced by its sponsors [9]; it does not establish that the platform will work in EMC.

**Purpose.** We assessed what current computational methods and available evidence establish about an EMC junction vaccine. We separated limitations of the disease from limitations of prediction methods and access to material. This analysis neither establishes that an EMC vaccine will work nor rules it out.

**Methods.** We reconstructed fusion transcripts while retaining the acceptor exon's untranslated sequence. We screened junction peptides with MHCflurry 2.1.4, models release 2.2.0 [2], and MHCnuggets [12]. Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) proteins display peptides to T cells. Class I and class II predictions were evaluated separately. We calculated predicted population coverage from Allele Frequency Net Database frequencies [1] and examined its dependence on allele panel, prediction threshold, predictor and population. Coverage describes carriage of an allele predicted to present a peptide; it does not measure presentation in a patient. We also searched the reviewed human proteome, including isoforms, for exact and near matches. Unreviewed entries were assessed separately. No wet-laboratory data were generated.

**Results.** Five of 27 declared exon pairs were in frame and produced 174 junction-spanning peptides. The initial class I screen identified 11 distinct predicted binders, including 4 strong binders. Four peptides also occurred in a normal *NR4A3* isoform. This finding removed one predicted binder but retained all 4 strong binders. The lead peptide was one residue from a self peptide; its immune recognition and cross-reactivity remain unknown.

Predicted coverage changed substantially with the screen. Pooling the in-frame junctions gave 27.4% on ten class I alleles and 30.4% on 34. On the wider panel, changing the presentation-percentile threshold from 0.2 to 0.5 to 2.0 changed coverage from 0% to 30.4% to 72.6%. An independently trained predictor gave 45.2% at its own conventional threshold on the same inputs. These figures are not biological ceilings or estimates with validated confidence intervals. The population and dependence analyses in Section 2.3 give separate bounds; none measures uncertainty in the predictions themselves.

The 23-allele class II screen identified one strong predicted binder. Predicted carriage of a presenting allele from each class was 1.8% under the stated independence assumption. The candidate synthetic long peptide contains 15 residues. Out-of-frame models produced stronger predictions, but they cannot encode the driver and are not proposed as EMC targets.

**Limitations.** We identified ten limitations involving the target, prediction methods, tumour microenvironment, material access and clinical development. Bulk RNA and limited spatial observations do not distinguish an immunologically quiet tumour from one that excludes T cells. We specify what evidence would change each conclusion without forecasting when it will arrive.

**Interpretation.** The main computational findings are the failure of a canonical-parent novelty filter at an isoform boundary and the strong dependence of predicted coverage on screening choices. These findings guide further assessment; they do not establish vaccine feasibility. Predicted binding is not evidence of tumour presentation, immunogenicity or benefit. The proposed combination rationale concerns this programme's own prior assessments and does not resolve the vaccine's antigen-related limitations. Nothing here supports use of any agent outside a clinical trial.

## Abstract

Extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma (EMC), a rare cancer, usually carries a join between the *EWSR1* and *NR4A3* genes. A vaccine might train T cells to recognize short protein fragments spanning that join. We asked what current computational methods can establish about this approach and what still requires experiments.

We reconstructed fusion sequences, screened their fragments and checked for matches in normal proteins. Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) proteins display fragments to T cells, and their inherited variants differ between people. We therefore estimated how many people carry an HLA variant predicted to display at least one candidate.

Four candidate fragments also occurred in an annotated normal *NR4A3* protein variant. Correcting this missed match removed one predicted binder; all four fragments classified as strong binders remained. A leading candidate differed from a normal protein fragment by just one amino acid. Whether T cells recognize it or cross-react with normal tissue is unknown.

Predicted population coverage changed from 0% to 72.6% when the acceptance threshold changed on the wider HLA panel. It also changed with the variants screened, prediction method and population. These figures describe model-dependent HLA carriage, not the proportion of patients whose tumors display a candidate or respond to vaccination.

The study identifies a failure in the original normal-protein check and shows why predicted coverage is not a biological limit. No laboratory data were generated. Actual tumor display, immune recognition, safety and benefit remain unmeasured; confirming the fusion sequence and testing those biological steps must precede a judgment of vaccine feasibility.

changes.after: **Evidence.** The ten-allele screen gives four strong peptide–allele calls over three predicted presenting alleles, with coverage of 27.4%. The 34-allele screen gives five strong calls over four predicted presenting alleles, with coverage of 30.4%. Both panels contain the same four distinct strongly predicted peptide sequences; a peptide can generate a call on more than one allele. Conversely, two peptides called on HLA-B\*15:01 do not add a second covered allele. Section 2.3 identifies every step and explains why five broad-panel calls produce four coverage steps. Section 7 reports the decoy comparison, against which this screen falls below expectation.

Coverage is computed by multiplying non-carrier frequencies across alleles, which assumes
independence both between loci and between alleles at the same locus. The same-locus case arises
here — two alleles pooled are both HLA-B — and handling it correctly moves the pooled figure by

changes.after: The headline coverage calculation multiplies non-carrier frequencies across alleles. It assumes independence between loci and approximates the dependence between alleles at the same locus. Two pooled alleles are both HLA-B; accounting for their shared locus moves the pooled value by about 0.3 percentage points. Actual dependence between loci was not measured or estimated from haplotype data. Possible coverage can nevertheless be bounded using the available marginal frequencies: §2.3 gives [17.5%, 29.9%] while retaining the within-locus assumption, and [9.2%, 31.1%] after also relaxing that assumption. Haplotype or genotype information could estimate the actual dependence or narrow the corresponding bounds. These bounds are not confidence intervals and do not quantify uncertainty in the peptide predictions.

## Abstract

Small tumour-expression studies can make unrelated gene sets appear higher in the tumour group. We tested whether those apparent increases exceeded what random gene sets of the same size would show on the same platform. This comparison is a *size-matched empirical null*: a reference distribution calculated by repeatedly scoring randomly selected genes.

In a series of 10 extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcomas (EMC) and 6 comparator sarcomas, an arbitrary set could yield t = 3.16 without differing from a size-matched random set. We applied the calibration to genes reported as direct targets of NR4A3 fusion proteins. A search of 2,276 retrieved documents identified three genes with a fusion DNA-binding assay: *SEMA3C*, *PPARG* and *ENO3*. Because three genes fall below the four-gene scoring floor, the scored aggregate combined them with sixteen native-NR4A3 targets.

On the two readable array platforms, that aggregate reached 39% and 88% of its null threshold and did not exceed either threshold. A published EMC expression signature exceeded its thresholds 11.9-fold and 4.2-fold in the same analyses. Individual-gene checks separated the candidates. *SEMA3C* failed the exact permutation tests and changed direction with comparator choice. *PPARG*'s strongest result reused its discovery cohort and was therefore not independent. *ENO3* survived the expression sensitivity analyses, but it was the pre-designated positive control; its elevation is not a new independent finding.

The central mechanistic gap remains. Our bounded search found no measurement of NR4A3-fusion binding or chromatin behaviour in EMC material. The available fusion experiment measures accessibility in HEK293T cells, while 110 NR4A peak sets concern a different protein or disease. No class-A gene showed unusual occupancy after comparison with the background panel. These data cannot distinguish expression associated with EMC from expression caused by the fusion. The calibration addresses a general failure mode in small studies with heterogeneous comparators; it does not establish fusion causation or clinical utility.

---
changes.after:
## Abstract

Small studies of rare cancers can make many unrelated groups of genes appear unusually active. We asked whether genes proposed to be controlled by NR4A3 fusion proteins in extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma (EMC) stood out from that background.

We compared the proposed group with randomly chosen groups of the same size, separately on each measurement platform. Only three genes had published assays showing an NR4A3 fusion binding DNA. Three was too few for the scoring method, so we grouped them with sixteen targets of the normal NR4A3 protein. This distinction matters: the combined group is not a set of nineteen demonstrated fusion targets.

The combined group did not exceed the random-group threshold on either of the two usable expression-array platforms. A previously published EMC expression signature exceeded both thresholds. Among the three genes, *SEMA3C* changed direction with the comparison tumors. *PPARG*'s strongest result reused the dataset in which it was discovered. *ENO3* remained elevated across the expression checks, but it had been designated as a positive control beforehand, so this is not an independent discovery.

Our bounded search found no measurements of NR4A3-fusion DNA binding in EMC material. Available binding measurements concern other proteins or tissues; two apparently positive comparisons did not survive correction for the number of comparisons. The cohorts are small and their comparison groups differ. These findings show why an attractive expression pattern needs a background comparison. They do not establish which genes the fusion causes to change. Binding and controlled fusion-perturbation experiments in EMC are needed to address that question.

---

changes.before: Higher expression in EMC has several possible explanations. The fusion could drive the gene. Alternatively, the expression could reflect EMC's cell of origin, its myxoid and hypocellular architecture, a platform-wide offset, a generic proliferation or matrix programme, or the anatomical site. The analysis tests parts of these alternatives but does not equate association with fusion causation.
changes.after: Higher expression in EMC could reflect an effect of the fusion. The alternative explanations are labelled here so that the comparisons below can refer to them consistently: **(a)** EMC's cell of origin; **(b)** its myxoid and hypocellular architecture, meaning abundant matrix and relatively few cells; **(c)** a platform-wide offset; **(d)** a generic proliferation or matrix programme; and **(e)** the anatomical site. The analysis tests parts of these alternatives but does not equate association with fusion causation.

## Appendix B · What would change this paper's conclusions

This is the current follow-up table. It separates missing experiments from analyses already completed in this working manuscript. Historical corrections remain in Appendix A.

| observation | implication and current status |
|---|---|
| An informative EWSR1::NR4A3 binding experiment in EMC showing no peak near *ENO3* | Would weaken evidence for binding within the assayed window and conditions. It would not rule out binding elsewhere, under other conditions, or indirect regulation by the fusion. |
| An EWSR1::NR4A3 binding experiment in EMC showing a peak near *SEMA3C* | Would supply binding evidence consistent with direct regulation despite the expression comparisons. Binding alone would not establish that the fusion causes the expression change; a controlled perturbation would address that separate question. |
| A fusion-positive EMC model with fusion knockdown and RNA-seq | Would test whether expression depends on the fusion and could change the ordering. Controls and the distinction between direct and indirect effects remain necessary. |
| An EMC expression series recording fusion type per sample | Would test whether *SEMA3C*'s comparator-dependence is really EWSR1-versus-TAF15 heterogeneity inside the EMC arm. |
| A soft-tissue normal comparator arm | Would address the cell-of-origin explanation, confound (a). A tissue comparison alone would not identify EMC's cell of origin or eliminate every lineage-related explanation. |
| Deep native NR4A3 ChIP-seq in human tissue | Already analysed: Haller's three acinic cell carcinomas and normal parotid sample provide the four deep Table 9 rows. They test the surrogate evidence in another disease; they do not supply fusion occupancy in EMC. |
| A broader per-arm reanalysis of GSE243553's barcode→variant files against a background panel | Remains distinct from the completed targeted *ENO3* accessibility comparison (§3.10). That four-site comparison did not exceed the geometry-preserving null (p = 0.08). A broader analysis would still concern accessibility in HEK293T, not fusion binding or causation in EMC. |
| A chromatin experiment deposited on EMC material under an indexed archive label | Would update the bounded retrieval result in §3.11. Its relevance to the mechanism would depend on whether it measured fusion binding or another chromatin property. The current search result is not proof that no unindexed experiment exists. |

null, taken from the *same* shuffled sequences so every exact figure is unchanged. *SEMA3C*'s window carries **39** one-mismatch sites, the most among the three class-A genes (*PPARG* 32, *ENO3* 28). It is not the highest count among all windows: 7 of the 198 background windows have at least 39, with a maximum of 43.

The count does not reject the composition-based explanation: the null mean is 33.7, with p = 0.203 against the dinucleotide-preserving shuffle and p = 0.118 in the GC-matched comparison. These non-significant results do not prove that composition explains the count. Only the raw panel rank, which does not account for composition, suggests enrichment (p = 0.040). *SEMA3C*'s window is the most AT-rich of the focus set (GC 0.371), while the NBRE is itself AT-leaning; GC-matching addresses that possible source of a high raw rank.

changes.after: **What the reader can check, and what would overturn it.** The four biological samples agree on the build; an error confined to one peak file would not account for all four readings. Agreement across samples cannot exclude a shared annotation error. We used the mark with the strongest prior expectation of promoter localisation. We did not use a transcription factor, because a factor that genuinely avoided promoters could mimic the wrong build. Build inference and occupancy calibration both rely on gene annotations and the assigned coordinates, despite using different resolved panels. A shared error could therefore affect both steps; identical panel membership or denominators are not assumed.
